title: Flip One Six to a Nine
statement:
You get a positive integer num whose digits are all 6 or 9. You may turn at most one digit upside down, so a 6 becomes a 9 or a 9 becomes a 6.

Return the largest number you can end up with. Leaving the number as it is counts as a valid choice.

examples.why: Turning the first 6 adds 3000. Turning the second 6 would only add 30.
The only 6 is the last digit, so that is the one to turn.
Every flip would make it smaller, so do nothing.

constraints: num consists only of the digits 6 and 9
hints: Turning a 9 into a 6 only ever makes the number smaller.
Turning a 6 into a 9 adds 3 times that digit's place value. Which 6 has the biggest place value?
Flip the leftmost 6, if there is one.

explain.intuition:
A flip from 6 to 9 adds 3 × place value, and a flip from 9 to 6 subtracts it. So the best move is the 6 with the highest place value: the leftmost 6. If there is no 6, any flip hurts and you keep the number.

In code, either replace the first "6" in the string form, or walk the digits with arithmetic and remember the place value of the highest 6 you see.
steps: Walk the digits from the right with a place value p starting at 1.
Whenever the digit is 6, record best = p. Later 6s overwrite earlier ones, so the leftmost wins.
Return num + 3 · best, where best is 0 if there was no 6.
pitfalls: Flipping the rightmost 6, which is what a right-to-left digit loop finds first if you stop at the first match.
Replacing every 6. Only one flip is allowed.

solutions.title: Replace the first 6 in the string
solutions.idea: The leftmost 6 has the biggest place value; string replace changes only the first match.

solutions.title: Digit arithmetic
solutions.idea: Find the place value of the leftmost 6 and add 3 times it.

followups: You may flip up to k digits. What changes?
Digits can now be any of 0–9 and a flip swaps 6 and 9 only. Does the greedy choice still hold?
